items.prompt: Name the four main word classes and state what each does in a sentence.
items.canonical_answer: A noun names (river, council, patience), a verb states an action or a being (floods, seemed), an adjective describes a noun (muddy river), and an adverb says how, when or where something happens, or modifies another word class (badly, tomorrow). The classes are a step towards analysis: the question is what the chosen class is doing in this sentence.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning of each class: noun names, verb states, adjective describes a noun, adverb modifies.
An answer that lists the classes with no sense of their jobs has defined nothing.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What do pronouns and determiners each do?
items.canonical_answer: Pronouns stand in for nouns already known (I, she, it, they), so a text need not repeat its names; determiners point a reader to which one is meant (the, this, some). The effect is closeness and economy: a repeated "she" keeps a person present without naming her again, and "this" presses the reader towards the thing under discussion.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: pronouns stand in for known nouns; determiners point to which one is meant.
Examples from the set given, or equally exact ones, are expected.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define lexis, and state what a lexical choice is.
items.canonical_answer: Lexis means the vocabulary of a text. A lexical choice is the choice of one word over its near-neighbours — "thin" over "skinny" or "slender" — and analysis asks why this word rather than that one, because near-neighbours carry different attitudes for the same fact.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the vocabulary of a text, and choice as the selection among near-neighbours.
The analysis question — why this word — should appear as part of the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is a semantic field, and what does a text use one for?
items.canonical_answer: A semantic field is a group of words from one area of meaning, such as water (rain, flood, drip, current). A text draws on a field to keep an idea in front of the reader: three or four words from one field inside a paragraph make the idea present even when no single sentence is about it.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: words from one area of meaning, grouped in a text.
Also credit what a text uses one for: keeping the idea before the reader.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Distinguish denotation from connotation, and state what a full analysis of a connotation must add.
items.canonical_answer: Denotation is what a word means; connotation is what it suggests beyond that. A full analysis adds the specific association and its effect on the reader: "the noun ‘leak’ suggests carelessness and neglect, so the reader blames maintenance, not rain." Calling a word positive or negative stops short of that and analyses nothing.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning of both terms, with the association named as what analysis must add.
An answer that stops at positive or negative connotations has not completed the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is a modifier, and how do a premodifier and a postmodifier differ in placement?
items.canonical_answer: A modifier adds detail to a noun or another word. A premodifier comes before it (a dry season) and a postmodifier after it (a season without rain). The placement changes pace: stacked premodifiers slow the reader before the noun arrives; a postmodifier makes them wait for it afterwards.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: detail added to a noun or verb, with premodifier before and postmodifier after.
The effect on pace is worth credit as the reason placement matters.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define metaphor, simile and personification, with one example each.
items.canonical_answer: Metaphor says one thing is another: "the town is a furnace." Simile says it is like another, using like or as: "the town lies like a furnace." Personification gives a non-human thing human actions or feelings: "the fog swallows the ridges." The three are told apart by their grammar: is, like, and a human action given to a non-human.
marking_guidance: Credit all three definitions with their distinguishing marks: is, like or as, human action to the non-human.
A definition without a separating mark has not defined the boundary.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is pathetic fallacy, and what work does it do in a text?
items.canonical_answer: Pathetic fallacy is a kind of personification in which weather or landscape is given human feeling, so the setting carries the mood: a sullen sky has done the atmosphere’s work before any person speaks. It matters because it lets a writer state an emotion without a person announcing it.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: weather or landscape given human feeling.
Also credit the work: the setting carries the mood, so emotion arrives without announcement.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Name the sound patterns a written text can carry, and give an example of each.
items.canonical_answer: Alliteration repeats initial consonants (hard, hot harvest); sibilance repeats s sounds (the slow sea slipped); plosives (b, p, t, k) strike sharply (the bucket banged); onomatopoeia imitates a sound (crackle, thud). In written text the reader hears these in the mind, which is why they work even on a silent page.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning of each term: alliteration, sibilance, plosives, onomatopoeia, each with an example.
The examples must actually carry the pattern named.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What does morphology study, and what does a coinage often signal?
items.canonical_answer: Morphology studies how words are built: prefixes and suffixes adjust meaning (un-, -less), compounds join two words (sunflower), and a coinage invents one. A coinage often signals informality or novelty, because a word the reader has not met makes the voice sound fresh and casual at once, as a blogger’s invented noun does.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: how words are built, from prefixes, suffixes, compounds and coinages.
The signal of a coinage — informality or novelty — is worth credit as part of the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a concrete and an abstract noun, and what does a shift between them do?
items.canonical_answer: A concrete noun names a thing the senses can reach (river, bread, needle); an abstract noun names an idea (patience, loss, freedom). A shift from one to the other changes what the reader is given to hold: a paragraph of concrete nouns lets the reader build a picture, and a turn to abstractions ("what remained was grief") asks them to think about what cannot be seen, so the shift itself carries the move from scene to meaning.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: sense-reachable things versus ideas.
Must say what a shift does: from picture to thought, which is the difference the reader feels.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this extract, written for the purpose: "The camp survived on tinned beans, borrowed paraffin and the kindness of strangers." How does the semantic field build the reader’s view of the camp?
items.canonical_answer: The nouns cluster in a field of scarcity and dependence: "tinned" and "borrowed" both carry the sense of stores that are not one’s own, and "kindness of strangers" completes the field by admitting that even the last resource is a gift. The words suggests a place living on other people’s margins, so the reader imagines the camp as fragile and grateful rather than self-sufficient, which prepares for whatever the piece asks them to feel about it.
marking_guidance: Must name the field: scarcity, dependence, gift.
Must trace the effect: the reader is led to see the camp as fragile and living on others, which the field builds word by word.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this sentence, written for the purpose: "The queue was a snake that inched and forked and finally slept." How does the metaphor shape the reader’s attitude to the queue?
items.canonical_answer: The metaphor makes the queue a living thing: "inched and forked and finally slept" gives it the slow movement, the splitting and the stillness of a reptile, and the tricolon of verbs carries the reader through its day in three beats. The reader is led to see the queue as a creature with its own will rather than a line of people, so the waiting becomes something happening to the town, not a choice anyone made — and the closing verb "slept" suggests a tiredness the reader can pity.
marking_guidance: Must name the metaphor by its word and phrase, and what it turns the queue into: a living creature with a will.
Must follow the effect on the reader: pity or resignation, produced by the creature’s verbs.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this sentence, written for the purpose: "The pot bubbled and spat, the fire hissed under it, and the whole kitchen crackled with appetite." How does the sound patterning reinforce the meaning?
items.canonical_answer: The pattern is a field of kitchen sounds built from onomatopoeia and plosives: "bubbled" and "spat" strike with short plosive beats, "hissed" adds sibilance, and "crackled" closes with a hard cluster that mimics the fire. The sound words suggests a kitchen alive and slightly aggressive, so the reader hears the cooking as appetite before the final noun names it, and the sentence’s meaning — food making its own fuss — is heard as well as read.
marking_guidance: Must name the sound patterns: onomatopoeia, plosives, sibilance, with the words that carry them.
Must say what the sound does: the reader hears the kitchen’s energy, so the meaning is reinforced by the ear.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this sentence, written for the purpose: "The office had gone fully paperless, or as my aunt calls it, aunt-proof." How does the coined word work on the reader?
items.canonical_answer: The coinage "aunt-proof" is built on the pattern of "waterproof" and "foolproof", so the reader hears a household word applied to an office policy, and the joke lands because the coinage compresses a whole argument — technology that excludes the older generation — into one invented adjective. The word suggests an informal, affectionate voice, one that can mock the policy without attacking anyone in it, so the reader is invited to laugh with the writer rather than judge the aunt.
marking_guidance: Must name the coined word and the pattern it borrows: foolproof, waterproof.
Must trace the effect: informality and affection, the reader laughing with the writer at the policy.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The word ‘squalid’ has negative connotations." What is missing, and what should replace the sentence?
items.canonical_answer: The error is stopping at the label: negative connotations names the direction of the association but not the association itself, so nothing has been analysed yet. The replacement names it: "squalid suggests dirt and neglect, so the reader blames the landlord and expects the piece to argue for repair." The specific association, and what it makes the reader feel or do, is the analysis.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: the label without the association.
Must give the fix: name the specific association and its effect on the reader.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner calls "the fog swallowed the ridge" a metaphor. What is wrong, and what test prevents it?
items.canonical_answer: The error is naming the wrong feature: the sentence says the fog did a thing — swallowed — which is personification, a human action given to a non-human thing; a metaphor would say the fog is something, as in "the fog is a grey animal." The test is to check the example against the definition before the label is written: personification gives actions, metaphor asserts identity, simile compares with like or as. A word named with the wrong feature undermines the point built on it.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: personification labelled as a metaphor.
Must give the test: check the example against the definition before naming it.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define grammatical voice, and name the two voices.
items.canonical_answer: Grammatical voice means whether a clause is active, with the doer as subject ("the council repaired the bridge"), or passive, with the thing acted on as subject ("the bridge was repaired"). It is not the same as a writer’s voice, which is the sense of a particular person speaking: one is a clause pattern, the other a presence on the page.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: active with the doer as subject, passive with the thing acted on as subject.
An answer that mixes the two senses of voice has taken the wrong term.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is aspect, and what does each of the progressive and the perfect present?
items.canonical_answer: Aspect is how an action is seen in time, whatever its tense. The progressive presents an action as ongoing ("the river is rising"); the perfect presents it as completed with present relevance ("the river has risen"). The choice tells the reader whether to watch something in motion or weigh something done.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: how an action is seen in time.
Both voices of aspect, progressive as ongoing and perfect as completed, are needed for the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the historic present, and what does it do for a reader?
items.canonical_answer: The historic present is the present tense used for past events: "Then the lights fail. Someone shouts." It pulls the reader into the scene as if it were unfolding, because the present tense promises this is happening now, so the reader waits with the people in the scene rather than hearing a report that everything is already over.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: present tense for past events.
The effect — immediacy, the reader made a witness — is what the definition is for.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define modality, and say what high and low modality each do.
items.canonical_answer: Modality is how far a writer commits: modal verbs and adverbs express certainty, possibility or obligation. High modality asserts ("this will work", "you must act"), which projects authority; low modality leaves room ("this may work", "you could act"), which sounds open and advisory. Each earns its effect against the text’s purpose and audience, so neither is right in general.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the degree of commitment, expressed by modal verbs and adverbs.
High as asserting, low as leaving room, is the contrast the definition needs.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between grammatical voice and a writer’s voice, and how can you keep them apart?
items.canonical_answer: Grammatical voice is whether a clause is active or passive, a pattern inside the sentence: "the gate was opened." A writer’s voice is the sense of a particular person speaking, carried by what they notice and how they say it, across a whole text. The test is scope: grammatical voice is decided clause by clause, a writer’s voice is heard paragraph by paragraph; and when an analysis says "the writer’s voice is passive here", the sentence has confused the two.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: a clause pattern versus a person’s presence on the page.
Must give the test: clause-by-clause decision versus the whole-text sense of a person.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this sentence, written for the purpose: "In the last audit, several payments were duplicated." How does the passive shape what the reader knows?
items.canonical_answer: The passive puts the payments in the subject’s seat and leaves the agent unstated, so the reader knows what happened but not who did it: "several payments were duplicated" hides or removes the doer, and the effect is that blame has nowhere to land. In an audit report that suits the writer, because the finding is on record and no colleague is named; the analysis says exactly that, which is what the label "passive" alone never says.
marking_guidance: Must name what the passive does to the words here: hides or removes the agent.
Must trace the effect: blame has nowhere to land, which serves a report that states findings without naming culprits.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Compare these two sentences, written for the purpose: "The bridge will be safe once the repairs are done" and "The bridge could be safe once the repairs are done." How does the change of modality alter the writer’s authority?
items.canonical_answer: The first is high modality: "will be" commits the writer to an outcome, so the reader hears an authority prepared to be answerable. The second is low modality: "could be" withdraws the commitment, so the reader hears caution or hedging. Against the purpose — an engineer writing to residents after a scare — the first builds trust and the second would raise it again, which is why the analysis of modality always names the audience the choice addresses.
marking_guidance: Must name the change in the modal words: high modality asserts, low modality leaves room.
Must say what each does for this reader: trust versus renewed doubt, against the purpose of reassuring residents.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this extract, written for the purpose: "My grandfather lifted the case, walked to the door, and stopped. He turns to me. He says nothing." How does the shift of tense work on the reader?
items.canonical_answer: The first two verbs are past ("lifted, walked"), narrating from a distance; then the extract shifts into the present ("turns, says"), and the shift makes events feel immediate, as if the reader has stepped into the memory beside the writer. The effect is that the remembered moment stops being a report and becomes a scene the reader is standing in, so the silence at the end is heard rather than summarised.
marking_guidance: Must name the shift of the verbs’ words: from past narration to the historic present.
Must trace the effect: immediacy — the reader moves from hearing a report to standing in the scene.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Rewrite this active sentence in the passive, then state what the change does: "The volunteers painted the mural on Sunday."
items.canonical_answer: The passive rewrite is: "The mural was painted on Sunday." The change removes the volunteers from the sentence: the action is on record, and the actor is not, so a reader asking who to credit has no answer. That suits a notice reporting the mural exists, and not an article celebrating the people who made it, which is the analysis to attach to the rewrite.
marking_guidance: Credit the passive rewrite: "The mural was painted on Sunday" or an equivalent that keeps the agent out.
Must state what the change does: the actor leaves the sentence, so credit or blame has nowhere to land.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define simple, compound and complex sentences.
items.canonical_answer: A simple sentence is one clause ("the bus came"). A compound sentence joins clauses of equal weight ("the bus came and the crowd moved"). A complex sentence carries one main clause with one or more dependent clauses ("when the bus came, the crowd moved"). The definitions are a step towards effect: equal weight beside unequal weight reads differently, and that is what the labels are for.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning of all three, with the clause structure of each.
The labels without the clause logic are half the card.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is a minor sentence, and how does it differ from a sentence fragment?
items.canonical_answer: A minor sentence is a deliberate fragment without a finite verb, used as a choice: "Not this time." A sentence fragment is the same shape by accident, an error rather than a choice. The difference is intention, and in analysis it matters: the first is a feature with an effect — a door closing — and the second is a slip that costs accuracy.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: a deliberate fragment without a finite verb.
The contrast with the accidental fragment — intention — is the difference that matters in analysis.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is syntax, and why does word order count as a choice?
items.canonical_answer: Syntax is the order of words in a sentence, and that order decides what the reader meets first and what waits. "The rain came down" makes the coming the fact; "down came the rain" makes the rain the news. Because the same words in a different order give the reader different news, word order is a choice with an effect, which is why analysis looks at it.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: word order in a sentence.
The reason it counts — first position decides emphasis — should be part of the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define fronting and its effect.
items.canonical_answer: Fronting moves an element to the start of a sentence, so the reader meets it first and gives it focus. "Down came the rain" fronts "down", and the rain’s arrival becomes the news; the everyday order would have buried the direction at the end. The effect is focus: whatever has been moved is what the sentence is now about.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: an element moved to the start for focus.
The effect on what the reader treats as the news is the definition’s purpose.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this extract, written for the purpose: "The valley filled with voices, with lorries, with the noise of a town waking all at once. Then silence." How does the final short sentence work on the reader?
items.canonical_answer: The long sentence piles clause on clause, three prepositional phrases and no full stop, so the reader is inside the noise with the town; then "Then silence." arrives, and the short sentence creates emphasis by contrast with the longer sentences around it. The effect is that the silence lands as an event, not an absence: after the variety and length of what came before, the two words stop the reader as abruptly as the valley was stopped, which is the mechanism.
marking_guidance: Must name the mechanism: the short sentence emphasised by contrast with the surrounding sentences.
Must trace the effect: the silence lands as an event, and the reader stops with the valley.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this sentence, written for the purpose: "They came for the wages, for the weather, for the last chance their generation would get." How does the list of three build weight?
items.canonical_answer: The list of three builds weight through its rhythm and its sense of completion: "for the wages, for the weather, for the last chance" repeats its opening, so each beat adds an item and the third closes the pattern with the phrase that matters most. The effect on the reader is the feeling that the causes have been counted and the count is finished, with the longest item last so its weight decides the sentence’s landing.
marking_guidance: Must name the tricolon by its words and rhythm: the repeated opening, the third beat closing the pattern.
Must say what the weight does: the reader feels the count is complete, with the decisive item last.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this sentence, written for the purpose: "Gone are the days when a letter took two weeks." How does the fronting shift the reader’s focus?
items.canonical_answer: The fronting puts "gone" first, so the reader meets the loss before they learn what has been lost, and the everyday order ("the days when a letter took two weeks are gone") would have buried the verdict at the end. The effect is that the sentence announces its conclusion in its first word, so the reader reads the rest already knowing the direction, which suits a writer opening with a judgement to make.
marking_guidance: Must name the fronting: "gone" moved to the front of the sentence.
Must trace the effect: the verdict arrives first, so the reader meets the loss before its subject.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between labelling a sentence type and analysing it, and what does the label alone never give?
items.canonical_answer: Labelling names the structure — simple, compound, complex — and stops at the grammar; analysing says what the structure makes this reader notice or feel at that point. A complex sentence at the moment of a flood carries cause and consequence in one breath, which is the point the label never reaches. The test is deletion: remove the label from the sentence, and if nothing about meaning or effect is left, nothing was analysed.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: the name of the structure versus what it does to this reader.
Must give the test: deletion of the label leaves either an effect or nothing.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The writer uses a complex sentence, then a simple sentence, then another complex sentence." What is missing, and how can the learner add it?
items.canonical_answer: The error is labelling without analysis: three labels are reported and no effect is named, so the reader of the answer learns nothing about the text. The fix is to add, after the labels, what the structures make this reader notice or feel here — the complex sentence holds the cause and the consequence together; the simple sentence that follows lands as a verdict — so each label is followed by its job at that point in the text.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: labels reported with no effect.
Must show the fix: after each label, what the structure makes the reader notice or feel at that point.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define structure as the term is used in analysis, and state what "structure" alone means.
items.canonical_answer: Structure means how a whole text is organised: its opening, sequence, shifts of focus, paragraphing and ending. Sentence structure is a feature of language, so the habit is to say "sentence structure" for that and let "structure" alone mean the whole text, which keeps the two levels from blurring in an analysis.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the organisation of a whole text.
The boundary with sentence structure should appear, so the two levels stay distinct.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is cohesion, and what ties does it include?
items.canonical_answer: Cohesion is the ties that link sentences and paragraphs so a text reads as one thing rather than a list. Its ties include discourse markers, reference and repetition: "however" turns the last sentence into a stepping stone, "this" picks it up, a repeated noun keeps one idea in front of the reader throughout.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the ties that link sentences and paragraphs.
The ties named — markers, reference, repetition — are what the definition is built from.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What does a discourse marker do? Give two examples.
items.canonical_answer: A discourse marker signals a step in the talk — however, meanwhile, first — rather than contributing content. "However" tells the reader a turn is coming; "meanwhile" holds one thread while another is picked up. The reader follows the route because the markers name the turns, which is why an analysis of a well-signposted text mentions them.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: a signal of a step, not a content word.
Two examples, with what each tells the reader, complete the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Distinguish anaphoric from cataphoric reference, and say what cataphoric reference creates.
items.canonical_answer: Anaphoric reference points back to something already mentioned ("the bridge… it"); cataphoric reference points forward ("this is what she saw: …"), creating an expectation the reader carries until it is met. The backward tie closes a loop the reader has already opened; the forward tie opens one, which is why a text that begins with cataphoric reference reads as a promise.
marking_guidance: Credit both meanings, with the backward and forward directions named.
The expectation cataphoric reference creates is the effect the definition exists for.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: List the structural features worth tracking in any non-fiction text.
items.canonical_answer: The features worth tracking are the opening and what it promises; shifts of focus, where the text turns from one thing to another; paragraph length, including any one-sentence paragraph; the sequence, what is told first and what waits; repetition across the text, an image or phrase that returns; and the ending, whether it resolves, echoes or stops. Each is a place a writer made a decision, which is why the list exists.
marking_guidance: Credit the features: opening, shifts of focus, paragraph length, sequence, repetition across the text, ending.
An answer that lists only paragraphing has taken one feature for the set.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this note about an extract, written for the purpose: "The account runs for four long paragraphs, tracing the search from boat to boat. Then, alone in its own paragraph: ‘At the third boat, they stopped looking.’" How does the one-sentence paragraph work?
items.canonical_answer: The one-sentence paragraph stands out against the long paragraphs around it, so it marks a turning point: the reader has been travelling with the search, boat by boat, and the isolated sentence changes what the journey means. The effect is that the reader stops too: the visual isolation of the line performs the stopping the words describe, which is why the writer set it alone.
marking_guidance: Must name the mechanism: a one-sentence paragraph isolated against longer ones.
Must trace the effect: it marks the turning point, and the isolation performs the stopping.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A piece about a reopened night market opens with the writer holding her grandmother’s hand in the same market thirty years before, and closes with her holding her own daughter’s hand in the same aisle. How does the cyclical structure shape the reader’s final view?
items.canonical_answer: The return to the opening image makes the ending feel like an arrival rather than a stop: the reader recognises the aisle and the held hand, and the difference between the two moments — grandmother replaced by daughter — is framed by the sameness around it. The effect is that the reader leaves the piece thinking about what lasts rather than what happened, which is what the cyclical structure exists to argue.
marking_guidance: Must name the cyclical structure in the text’s own words and images: the ending returns to the opening image.
Must say what the return does: the reader weighs what changed against what lasted, and the ending lands as an arrival.

items.prompt: In an analysis, what does structure cover and what does language cover, and how do you keep them apart?
items.canonical_answer: Structure covers the organisation of the whole text: what opens it, what follows, where the turns are, what ends it. Language covers the choices inside sentences: words, images, grammar, sentence structure, sound. The test is scope: if the point is about where something sits and in what order, it is structure; if it is about the words themselves, it is language. A paragraph about paragraphing is not a language point, and a paragraph about metaphor is not a structure point.
marking_guidance: Must state what each heading covers: whole-text arrangement versus word-level and sentence-level choices.
Must give the test: where-and-order versus the words themselves.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The rescue is described in the final paragraph, which is near the end." What is wrong with this as a structural point, and what would replace it?
items.canonical_answer: The error is location without effect: the sentence says where the paragraph is and says nothing about what the arrangement does. The replacement names the arrangement and its effect: "the account of the rescue is held back until the final paragraph, so the reader spends the piece asking whether it succeeded, which is how the piece creates suspense." The arrangement plus the reader’s experience of it is the analysis; the arrangement alone is a map reference.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: saying where things are without what the arrangement does.
Must give the replacement: arrangement plus effect on this reader.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What does first-person narration give a text, and what does it take away?
items.canonical_answer: First-person narration is told by an "I" inside the story. It gives closeness — the reader stands inside one mind and feels what it feels — and it takes away knowledge: the reader knows only what that narrator knows, so the writer can surprise them with the narrator or mislead them by the narrator, and both are effects to analyse.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning of first person and what it gives: closeness, a single mind.
Credit what it takes away: knowledge limited to what the narrator knows.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is second-person address, and what does it do to the reader?
items.canonical_answer: Second-person address puts the reader inside the text as "you": "You walk in and the smell of fresh paint meets you at the door." It involves the reader directly, making them the person the events happen to, and it can press them towards a choice, because instructions and warnings in the second person are hard to feel exempt from.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the reader placed in the text as "you".
The effect — involvement, and pressure towards what the writer wants — is the definition’s purpose.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Distinguish limited third-person narration from omniscient narration.
items.canonical_answer: Third-person narration is limited when it stays with one character’s knowledge ("Klaas did not know what waited at the top") and omniscient when it moves freely and reports what no single character could know ("none of them knew that the road had already been closed"). The choice decides what the reader is allowed to know, which is why an analysis of perspective starts by asking which of the two is working.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning of both kinds, with the knowledge each allows.
The boundary is knowledge: one mind’s horizon versus the narrator’s freedom.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between the narrator and the author, and why does the difference matter in analysis?
items.canonical_answer: The narrator is the voice inside the text, a construct made of sentences; the author is the person who wrote it, who may share none of the narrator’s views. The difference matters because a first-person narrator who is wrong, prejudiced or unkind is a choice the author made, and analysing that gap is often the point: the reader is invited to see further than the "I" can. Treating the narrator’s opinion as the author’s erases the most interesting thing about the narration.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: the voice inside the text versus the person who wrote it.
Must say why: the gap between them is a choice to analyse, not an error to correct.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A story is narrated by a farmhand who describes a new owner’s changes with pride, while the reader watches the workers’ unease grow around him. How does the first-person narration limit what the reader knows, and what does that make the reader do?
items.canonical_answer: The narration limits the reader to the farmhand’s understanding: his account reports what he sees with pride, and the unease of the others reaches the reader mainly through what he notices of it, which the reader can read further than he can. The effect is that the reader works: they read past the narrator, putting the story together against his reading of it, and the dramatic irony — the reader knowing more than the "I" — becomes the story’s engine, which the first-person choice created.
marking_guidance: Must name the limit in the extract’s words: knowledge confined to the narrator, who sees less than the reader infers.
Must say what the reader does: reads past the narrator and assembles the unease the "I" misses.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner calls every first-person extract "stream of consciousness". What is wrong, and what test fixes it?
items.canonical_answer: The error is using the term loosely: stream of consciousness is a continuous, unpunctuated flow of a mind as it thinks, not any first-person account. The test is the defining feature: does the extract reproduce the movement of thought itself, without the tidying of finished sentences? A calm, well-shaped first-person memory is not stream of consciousness, and the label undermines the point built on it.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: the term used without its defining feature.
Must give the test: the unpunctuated flow of thought itself, or the label does not apply.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define a rhetorical question and state how it works on an audience.
items.canonical_answer: A rhetorical question expects no answer, because the answer is assumed. It works by making the audience supply the answer the writer wants: having said "no" in their own head, the reader has joined the writer’s side before the argument begins. That is why an analysis of one names the answer it invites, or it has said nothing the label did not.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: a question expecting no answer, because the answer is assumed.
The mechanism — the reader supplies the wanted answer — is the definition’s working part.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is direct address, with an example?
items.canonical_answer: Direct address uses you or your to put the reader in the sentence: "You have three days to register." The reader stops being an onlooker and becomes the person the sentence is about, which is why advertisements, warnings and appeals reach for it whenever the next step is the reader’s to take.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: you or your placing the reader in the sentence.
An example with the reader put in the sentence completes the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define tricolon, anaphora, antithesis and hyperbole, with one example each.
items.canonical_answer: A tricolon is a list of three with a rhythm that builds to a close ("for the wages, for the weather, for the last chance"); anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses ("we came, we saw, we stayed"); antithesis sets opposed ideas in balance ("made by history, unmade by a season"); hyperbole exaggerates for effect ("the queue stretched to the moon"). Each works by its pattern, which is what the analysis names.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning of all four, each with a distinguishing example.
Definitions without examples have named the devices without showing their patterns.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is anaphora, and what does the repetition give a piece?
items.canonical_answer: Anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses: "We were told to wait. We were told the road was coming. We were told again." The repetition gives the piece a drumbeat, so the reader feels accumulation rather than hearing a list, and the effect is pressure: by the third beat the reader is waiting for the pattern to break, which is where the writer places the change that matters.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: repetition at the start of successive clauses.
The effect — accumulation and pressure towards the break — is what the definition is for.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define antithesis and give an example of its effect.
items.canonical_answer: Antithesis sets opposed ideas in balance: "made by history, unmade by a season." The balanced grammar makes the two halves weigh equal, so the reader holds them together and feels the loss inside the shape, and the effect is clarity of contrast: what is won on one side and lost on the other is visible in the sentence’s own architecture.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: opposed ideas set in balanced grammar.
The effect — the contrast made visible in the shape — completes the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is hyperbole, and what does it offer that a plain statement does not?
items.canonical_answer: Hyperbole exaggerates for effect: "the queue stretched to the moon" rather than "the queue was long". It offers the reader an attitude rather than a measurement: the exaggeration signals that the writer’s feeling is the point, and the reader shares the feeling — the absurdity, the exasperation — rather than checking the figure. Used well it is comedy or outrage; used carelessly it is inflation the reader stops believing.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: exaggeration for effect, not measurement.
The trade it offers — attitude rather than figure — is the definition’s purpose.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this sentence, written for the purpose: "Should a child’s first classroom be a corridor with no roof?" How does the rhetorical question position its audience?
items.canonical_answer: The question expects no answer, because the answer it invites is "no", and the reader who supplies that "no" has condemned the corridor before the piece argues anything. The words "a child’s first classroom" position the audience as people responsible for children, and the absurdity of "no roof" supplies the outrage, so the question works by making the reader the one who says the damning thing, which is the mechanism to analyse.
marking_guidance: Must name the invited answer in the question’s words: no, and the reader made to say it.
Must say what the question does to this audience: positions them as responsible and extracts the verdict before the argument.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: How does a rhetorical question differ from a question that expects an answer, and what is the test?
items.canonical_answer: A rhetorical question expects no answer, because the answer is assumed and the question is there to make the audience supply it; a genuine question wants information — "what time does the bus leave?" — and waits for a reply. The test is what the text does next: a question the text goes on to answer, or that seeks information the writer does not have, is not rhetorical, whatever it looks like.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: assumed answer versus sought information.
Must give the test: whether the text answers it, or waits for a reply.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner labels two questions rhetorical: "Why do we tolerate this?" and, two lines later, "What is to be done? The council has three options." What is wrong, and how could the learner check?
items.canonical_answer: The error is calling every question rhetorical without testing it. The first expects no answer and invites the reader’s agreement, so it is rhetorical. The second is answered by the text itself two words later — "three options" — so it is a signposting question, a way of announcing structure, not a rhetorical one. The check is what the text does next: if the text answers it, or genuinely seeks information, the label is wrong, and treating rhetorical questions as the only rhetorical device misses anaphora, antithesis and the rest of the set.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: the label applied without the test.
Must apply the test to both questions: answered by the text, so not rhetorical; and note the wider point that rhetorical devices are more than questions.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define tone, and state what an analysis of tone must do.
items.canonical_answer: Tone is the attitude a text conveys towards its subject or reader, such as urgent, wry or reassuring. It is a result of choices, not a thing in itself, so an analysis of tone must name the choices that create it: a wry tone is made of understatement and a dry aside, and the reader’s smile is the effect of those, which is what naming "wry" alone never shows.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the attitude a text conveys towards its subject or reader.
The requirement to name the choices that create the tone is part of the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is register, and what decides whether a formal one fits?
items.canonical_answer: Register is the variety of language suited to a situation, marked chiefly by formality and vocabulary. A formal register is right or wrong only for an audience and a purpose: it suits a report to officials, and it mismatches a blog written for friends exactly as a casual register would mismatch the report. That is why an analysis of register always names the audience and purpose it is judged against.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the variety of language suited to a situation.
The judgement by audience and purpose, not in general, is the definition’s centre.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is formality, and what features mark its two sides?
items.canonical_answer: Formality is how far language follows formal public usage rather than casual private usage. The informal side is marked by contractions, slang, the first person and spoken markers ("look, we just thought"); the formal side by nominalisation and Latinate vocabulary ("the implementation of remediation"). The two sides are a scale, not a switch, and a text can sit anywhere along it.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the scale between formal public and casual private usage.
Markers on both sides — contractions and slang against nominalisation and Latinate vocabulary — complete the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define pragmatics and implicature.
items.canonical_answer: Pragmatics is the study of meaning that comes from context and implication, not from the words alone; implicature is what a writer implies without stating it. "The meeting ended early" states a fact, and in a context where the meeting was expected to fail, it implies a judgement without a single evaluative word: the reader does the concluding.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning of both terms, with implication rather than statement as the key.
The analysis work — reading what is implied — is what the definitions are for.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is an implicature, and how is it identified in a text?
items.canonical_answer: An implicature is what a writer implies without stating it. It is identified by the gap between what the words say and what the situation makes them mean: "I read the first chapter" — asked about a whole book — implies the rest went unread, and the reader hears the verdict the writer never wrote. The analysis names the implication and the context that produces it.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: what is implied without being stated.
The identification — the gap between words and situation — is the definition’s use.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between tone and register, and how can one text carry both separately?
items.canonical_answer: Register is the variety of language suited to a situation, marked chiefly by formality and vocabulary; tone is the attitude a text conveys towards its subject or reader. A text can be formal in register and warm in tone — a council notice written kindly for a purpose of soothing — or informal and bitter, so the two are separate axes: one answers "what situation is this language for, and for which audience and purpose?", the other "what attitude does it carry?". A reader told a text is "formal and friendly" has been given both, correctly — with the audience and purpose that make each register the fitting one for a situation named beside it.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: situation-suited variety versus conveyed attitude.
Must show they are separate axes: register does not decide tone, and a text can carry any pairing of the two.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between how common a word is and how formal it is, and why must analysis keep them apart when judging a text’s fit for its audience and purpose?
items.canonical_answer: Commonness is frequency: everyday words against rare ones. Formality is register: public-usage words against casual ones, judged against the audience and purpose a text serves. The two do not move together — "the committee met" is common and formal; a slang coinage can be rare and informal — so an analysis that calls an everyday word casual, or a rare word formal, has merged two scales into one and lost the evidence. Ask them separately: is the word everyday or rare, and is it formal or informal.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: frequency versus formality, two scales.
Must give the separate questions and a pair that breaks the link between them.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this sentence, written for the purpose: "Perhaps we could look again at the question of the paint." What does the sentence imply beyond its words?
items.canonical_answer: On the surface the sentence is a polite suggestion about timing; the implicature is that the paint decision is wrong and should be revisited. The detail "look again" implies the first decision was badly made, and "perhaps we could" softens what is, in fact, a disagreement, so the reader hears a correction dressed as a request, which is the pragmatic work of the sentence: the writer avoids the blame the plain statement would carry.
marking_guidance: Must name the implication one detail carries: the decision was wrong and should be revisited.
Must tie the reading to the wording that suggests it: "look again" and the softening "perhaps we could", which let a disagreement arrive as a request.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read this extract, written for the purpose: "The scheme was implemented across three wards. Attendance rose by a fifth. And look — we were as surprised as you are." How does the shift of register signal a change in the writer’s relationship with the reader?
items.canonical_answer: The extract opens in a formal register — "implemented", the passive, the statistic — which keeps the writer at the distance of an official reporting; then "And look — we were as surprised as you are" drops into contractions, direct address and the first person plural, and the shift signals a change in the relationship: the writer steps out from behind the report and admits the reader to confidence. The effect on the reader is companionship after formality, which makes the statistic land as news between equals rather than a finding from above.
marking_guidance: Must name the shift in the extract’s words: from formal report register to conversational, direct address.
Must trace the effect on the reader: admitted to confidence, so the statistic lands between equals.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The word ‘melancholy’ is rare, so the text is formal and the tone is sad." What three questions has the learner collapsed into one, and what is the answer here?
items.canonical_answer: The learner has collapsed commonness, formality and tone into one idea. The three questions asked separately: is "melancholy" everyday or rare? (rare); is it formal or informal? (formal, but a rare word can be slang — the scales do not move together); and what attitude do the choices add up to? ("melancholy" is itself a tone word, but the tone of the passage depends on the rest of the choices, not on one word’s rarity). The sentence as written draws two conclusions from one piece of evidence, and neither follows.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake and the three separate questions: frequency, formality, tone.
Must answer them separately for this word, showing that rarity does not settle formality and neither settles tone.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt:
Read this extract, written for the purpose:

The last shop opened its shutters with a sound like a yawn. Inside, the bread stand stood bare except for one flat loaf, grey as a Monday. Mrs Kambazembi wiped the counter in slow circles, and the cloth squeaked against the wood, a small tired song. The shelves behind her held nothing but labels now: they were the last honest things in the shop. Outside, the street was so quiet that we could hear the river drying.

Identify and analyse three word-level features (word class, semantic field, figurative language, sound patterning or word formation), each with its evidence and its effect on the reader.
items.canonical_answer:
The extract builds a field of exhaustion and emptiness. "Bare", "grey", "nothing but labels" and "so quiet" cluster around absence, and the words suggest a shop at the end of its life, so the reader arrives at the piece’s subject — decline — before any sentence states it.

Figurative language carries the mood without naming it. The simile "like a yawn" gives the shutters a human tiredness, and the metaphor "grey as a Monday" borrows the flattest day of the working week for the loaf’s colour; the personification "a small tired song" lets the cloth sing the weariness the shopkeeper does not voice, and the reader is given the mood as something the room itself performs.

The sound patterning is a quiet reinforcement: "slow circles" and "cloth squeaked" pair sibilance with the onomatopoeia of "squeaked", so the ear follows the wiping as it happens. The final clause personifies the river — "we could hear the river drying" — and it is the only clause where the narration reaches outside the shop, which makes the drying river the context for everything inside: the emptiness is not the shop’s alone.
marking_guidance: Credit three word-level features, each identified from the extract’s own words: credit the class, field, figure or sound named as evidence.
Credit the effect of each on the reader, tied to the words that produced it, so the words quoted are the evidence and the analysis the effect.
A feature named without the words or without its effect is spot-naming, not analysis.
The model paragraphs are the standard: three features, evidence and effect each, organised by the reading the features build.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt:
Read this extract, written for the purpose:

Your morning, solved. One twist of the cap and the Smokliq drips sunshine straight into your veins — grapefruit, ginger and green rooibos, cold-steeped overnight in our Windhoek kitchen. No sugar. No apologies. Our bottles are washed, refilled and washed again, because the planet is thirsty too. Grab a Smokliq on your way to anywhere, and let your tongue do the waking up.

Identify and analyse three word-level features (word class, semantic field, figurative language, sound patterning or word formation), each with its evidence and its effect on the reader.
items.canonical_answer:
The vocabulary is built from imperative verbs and second-person address: "Grab", "let your tongue do the waking up" put the reader inside the advertisement as the person who acts, and each imperative suggests that buying is the natural next movement of the reader’s morning.

The coinage "Smokliq" and the invented compound "cold-steeped" signal novelty: a named brand that sounds liquid and smoked at once gives the product an identity the reader can hold, and the unusual compound suggests a craft process rather than a factory one, which flatters the reader’s taste.

The sound patterning sells freshness: "grapefruit, ginger and green rooibos" is a tricolon carried on alliteration and plosives, so the ingredients strike the ear as lively. The personification "drips sunshine straight into your veins" is hyperbole riding a metaphor, and its effect is to make the drink perform an impossible service — daylight, injected — which the reader takes as energy, not as a claim to check.
marking_guidance: Credit three word-level features, each identified from the extract’s own words: credit the class, field, figure or sound named as evidence.
Credit the effect of each on the reader, tied to the words that produced it, so the words quoted are the evidence and the analysis the effect.
A feature named without the words or without its effect is spot-naming, not analysis.
The model paragraphs are the standard: three features, evidence and effect each, organised by the reading the features build.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt:
Read this extract, written for the purpose:

Flood waters receded across the Oshana region last night, and assessment teams reached the three cut-off villages by boat this morning. Two shelters have been opened at the Ompundja primary school. Four hundred and ten households have been registered for support, and the regional council has confirmed that the bridge on the D- road will remain closed while the supports are inspected. The water is expected to fall steadily over the coming days.

Identify and analyse three word-level features (word class, semantic field, figurative language, sound patterning or word formation), each with its evidence and its effect on the reader.
items.canonical_answer:
The extract is organised around the passive voice and the numbers. "Flood waters receded" is active, but from there the human actors are removed: "Two shelters have been opened", "the bridge… will remain closed" — the passive hides or removes the agents, so the reader is told what is being done without being told who is doing it, which is the register of an official bulletin distributing reassurance.

Modality is low and deliberate: "is expected to fall steadily" commits to nothing the council can be blamed for if it is wrong, and "confirmed" asserts certainty about the closure while the river’s behaviour stays hedged. The reader receives an account in which official actions are fact and natural ones are forecast.

The sentence structures are short and declarative, one fact per clause, with fronted prepositional phrases ("Inside the region", "By boat") mapping the geography as the sentences move; the compound sentences join facts without subordinating them, so no fact reads as more important than another except by position, and the newest information — the falling water — is given last as the reader’s takeaway.
marking_guidance: Credit grammatical analysis of voice (active and passive, with agents named or removed), tense or aspect, and modality, each with the words that show it.
Credit sentence-structure analysis: type, length, order and their effect on this reader, with the words quoted as evidence.
A label without its effect is not analysis; the model’s final sentence pattern, feature, evidence, effect, is the shape to reward.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt:
Read this extract, written for the purpose:

On the day the letter came, I was mending the pen fence with wire and a stone for a hammer. My hands knew the work. That is what I remember thinking, that my hands knew the work and nothing else did, because the letter sat inside my shirt like a coal that would not cool. My mother had waited eleven years for that envelope. I walked it up the hill without opening it, and the wind pulled my hair across my face so I could not see the gate.

Identify and analyse three word-level features (word class, semantic field, figurative language, sound patterning or word formation), each with its evidence and its effect on the reader.
items.canonical_answer:
The narration is first person and retrospective, and the aspect choices slow the moment: "was mending" (progressive) holds the action ongoing so the reader stands inside it, while "my hands knew the work" (perfect) states a completed state of knowledge, and the contrast suggests a mind half in the task and half on the letter.

The simile "sat inside my shirt like a coal that would not cool" carries the extract’s tension: the coal is heat that persists, so the letter reads as something that cannot be put down, and the reader braces for its opening.

The sentence structures are long and subordinated where the waiting is felt — "that my hands knew the work and nothing else did" nests the thought inside the remembered one — and then the final long sentence turns the world against the reader: "the wind pulled my hair across my face so I could not see the gate" ends the extract with the gate withheld, so the syntax performs the not-seeing the sentence describes.
marking_guidance: Credit grammatical analysis of voice (active and passive, with agents named or removed), tense or aspect, and modality, each with the words that show it.
Credit sentence-structure analysis: type, length, order and their effect on this reader, with the words quoted as evidence.
A label without its effect is not analysis; the model’s pattern, feature, evidence, effect, is the shape to reward.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt:
Read this extract, written for the purpose:

Friends, colleagues, and one very brave teacher in the third row — good evening.
Tonight I want to talk about the swimming pool. Not the pool we have. The pool we were promised.
Nine years ago, a plan was drawn for this town. It had a pool, a library wing and a hall with a proper stage. We got the parking. We got the parking very well.
So what went wrong? You know what went wrong. The money went the way money goes when nobody is watching.
But here is the good news, and I will be quick, because the choir has been patient. This year the council has a surplus. A real one. Audited. And I am asking — not demanding, asking — that we finish what was drawn.
Swim with me on this.
Thank you.

Identify and analyse three word-level features (word class, semantic field, figurative language, sound patterning or word formation), each with its evidence and its effect on the reader.
items.canonical_answer:
The speech is built for listeners, and its structure is signposted for ears: the greeting names the audience directly ("Friends, colleagues, and one very brave teacher"), the tricolon in the opening and the repeated "We got the parking" give the listener beats to hold, and the closing pun "Swim with me on this" lands the argument in one line the hall can carry home.

The perspective is a named speaker arguing a case: the first person governs, and the direct address "You know what went wrong" makes the audience co-authors of the blame, an effect of the second-person reach inside a first-person speech. The rhetorical question is answered by the speaker himself, so it works as a pause for agreement rather than a genuine enquiry.

The tone moves from wry to urgent to warm, and the moves are made by register shifts: "the money went the way money goes when nobody is watching" is the formal charge dressed as a proverb, and "I am asking — not demanding, asking —" is a deliberate drop into humility that positions the surplus as a favour to be granted, which the audience is left feeling able to give.
marking_guidance: Credit analysis of whole-text structure: the opening, shifts of focus, paragraph length and sequence, each with the words that show the arrangement and its effect on the listener or reader.

items.prompt:
Read this extract, written for the purpose:

Right, so: houseplants. I said last month that I would not buy another one, and I want to begin by admitting that I now own six.
What changed? A friend of mine — you know who you are — gave me a cutting in a jam jar, and something in my brain simply broke.
Here is the thing nobody tells you about plant people. It is hardly about the plants. It is about the mornings. It is about walking past a shelf and finding a new leaf that was not there on Monday, and feeling, briefly, like a competent person.
My grandmother grew a whole garden on spite and bathwater, so I cannot claim talent runs in the family. But the joy is transferable.
Buy the cutting. Water it when you remember. That is the whole discipline, and it is more than enough.

items.canonical_answer:
The blog post’s structure is a confession turned argument: the opening concedes the opposite of the post’s thesis ("I said last month that I would not buy another one"), and the turn comes at "Here is the thing", a discourse marker that tells the reader the real subject is arriving. The final section converts the confession into advice, and the short imperative sentences ("Buy the cutting. Water it when you remember.") close the piece as a gift rather than a boast.

The perspective is a first-person voice in conversation with its readers: the direct address "you know who you are" and the invented shared reader "plant people" build a community the reader is invited into, and the aside in dashes performs the intimacy the register claims.

The tone is self-deprecating comedy built on understatement and a register that mixes informal contractions with a mock-epic gravity ("something in my brain simply broke"). The allusion to the grandmother "grew a whole garden on spite and bathwater" is hyperbole with affection in it, so the reader laughs with the writer rather than at the hobby, which is the post’s purpose fulfilled.
